author: Becky Upham
title: 7 Ways to Cope With Digital Eyestrain if You Have Dry Eye - NewsBreak
text:
By Becky Upham Edmund Tsui ,
1 days ago If your day requires spending long stretches of time in front of a computer, phone, or tablet, all that screen time can make chronic dry eye symptoms even worse. Dry eye , formally known as keratoconjunctivitis sicca or lacrimal keratoconjunctivitis, develops when your eyes don't make enough tears or your tears evaporate too quickly. As a result, your eyes may feel irritated, gritty, watery, or blurry.
Too much screen time can also lead to digital eyestrain, the name for temporary eye discomfort and vision problems linked to the use of digital devices. If you already have dry eye, that added strain can make your symptoms more noticeable and make it harder to work, read, or get through a screen-heavy day.
When you concentrate your sight on a screen, you blink less often and may not close your eyes completely, says Catherine Heyman, OD , the founding dean and an associate professor at the school of optometry at High Point University in High Point, North Carolina. "Blinking less makes tears evaporate more quickly, leaving the eyes dry and irritated," she says.
Digital eyestrain (aka computer vision syndrome ) is temporary, but the pain, irritation, and blurry vision can still make it hard to concentrate, get your work done, or simply get through the day. The good news: A few simple, expert-recommended changes can ease your discomfort and make screen-heavy days more manageable.
1. Take Regular Screen Breaks When we use screens, we don't blink enough and our eyes get dry, says Michelle Andreoli, MD , an ophthalmologist at Northwestern Medicine in the Chicago area and a spokesperson for the American Academy of Ophthalmology .
"We normally blink about 15 times in one minute, but only about 5 to 7 times in a minute while using computers, phone screens, or watching TV. That's why looking at screens for long periods of time without taking breaks may cause eyestrain, which can feel like ‘tired eyes,' and symptoms like dry eyes, blurry vision , or headaches," says Dr. Andreoli.
That's why it's important to take breaks frequently when using screens for long periods of time, she says.
Try the 20-20-20 rule: Every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away for at least 20 seconds. If you need help remembering, Andreoli suggests setting a timer or using an app.
2. Practice Slow, Complete Blinks Blinking less isn't the only problem. When you concentrate your vision on a computer, phone, or other digital device's screen, your blinks are often incomplete, says Dr. Heyman. Your upper eyelid doesn't come all the way down across your eye, leaving part of the eye's surface exposed.
That's an issue because a complete blink is necessary to spread the tear film evenly across the surface of the eye, she says.
Use each screen break as a reminder to blink slowly and completely several times, Heyman says. To practice full blinking exercises, gently close your eyes for two seconds, open them, close them gently for another two seconds, then squeeze your eyelids together for two seconds before opening them again.
3. Position Your Screen Slightly Lower The position of your screen can also contribute to dryness, says Heyman.
"I recommend positioning the computer monitor slightly below eye level, which reduces how widely the eyes must remain open and may slow tear evaporation," she says. If needed, increase the font size rather than leaning closer, says Heyman.
Andreoli recommends sitting 25 inches (about two feet) away.
4. Reduce Glare and Make the Screen Easier to Read You may not realize it, but glare, low contrast, and small text make your eyes work harder to see what's on the screen.
Little changes like adjusting the brightness and contrast and minimizing glare can make the screen easier to see and reduce eyestrain, says Andreoli. Your device's system settings will allow you to adjust brightness to a comfortable level and increase contrast. And you can minimize glare by blocking light that reflects onto your screen by closing window curtains or blinds, and by avoiding harsh overhead lighting and using lower-wattage bulbs.
Increasing the font size and alternating computer work with non-screen tasks can also help, says Heyman.
If you're considering blue-light-blocking glasses , keep your expectations in check. "The American Academy of Ophthalmology does not recommend blue-light-blocking glasses because there is no evidence that they help alleviate eyestrain," says Andreoli.
5. Keep Fans and Vents Aimed Away From Your Face Fans , heating vents, air-conditioning, and low humidity can cause tears to evaporate more quickly, adding to screen-related dryness, says Heyman.
"People should avoid having fans or air vents directed toward their faces and consider using a humidifier in particularly dry environments," she says. Check the airflow around your usual workspace and redirect a vent or move your seat if needed, says Heyman.
6. Use Artificial Tears Before Discomfort Builds Eye drops , or artificial tears can add moisture when reduced blinking leaves your eyes dry during screen use. "They should be used proactively, such as before an extended period of computer work, rather than waiting until the eyes become extremely uncomfortable," says Heyman.
If you find yourself reaching for drops more than four times a day, she generally recommends preservative-free artificial tears, as preservatives may cause additional irritation with repeated use. Preservative-free drops can be used as often as needed.
If you have severe dry eyes, Andreoli suggests asking your ophthalmologist about a prescription for a thicker gel or ointment.
Contact lens wearers should make sure the drops are approved for use with them, says Heyman.
She advises against relying on products marketed mainly to "get the red out," because they may not adequately treat dryness and can sometimes cause rebound redness.
"Perhaps most importantly, people should keep in mind that while artificial tears help manage symptoms, they may not address the underlying cause of dry eye ," says Heyman.
7. Know When to See an Eye Doctor You shouldn't assume that discomfort and fluctuating vision are simply part of the deal if you spend most of your day looking at screens, says Heyman.
If symptoms continue even after you've made changes like those previously mentioned, an eye exam could help uncover the cause, she says. "Dry eye is not a single condition; it can be related to eyelid inflammation, problems with the oil-producing glands in the eyelids, medication side effects, contact lens wear, autoimmune disease, environmental factors, or other eye conditions," says Heyman.
If your symptoms are affecting productivity, comfort, or quality of life, it is time to schedule an eye examination, she says.
Eye pain, significant redness, light sensitivity, discharge, a sudden change in vision, an eye injury, or the feeling that something is stuck in your eye shouldn't be brushed off or something to discuss at a future appointment; you should seek care right away for any of those symptoms , says Heyman.
The Takeaway A condition called dry eye can develop when your eyes don't make enough tears, or your tears evaporate too quickly. Screen time can worsen dry eye, because people tend to blink less often and less completely while using digital devices. Tactics like regular screen breaks, slow and complete blinks, and display adjustments can make screen-heavy days more comfortable. Schedule an eye exam if symptoms persist or interfere with daily life, and seek prompt care for eye pain, significant redness, light sensitivity, discharge, an injury, or a sudden change in vision.
